title: OBBBA Medicaid Work Requirements + ACA Subsidy Cliff Compound
activeNode: One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1 / P.L. 119-21)
catalyst: P.L. 119-21, signed July 4, 2025, mandates 80 hrs/month Medicaid work requirements for the ACA expansion population across 40 states + DC by Jan 1, 2027 (CMS interim final rule, June 1, 2026); several states are implementing earlier on their own timelines. It lands the same year the separate, IRA-era enhanced ACA premium tax credits expired (Dec 31, 2025, and still unrenewed by Congress when 2027 open enrollment began Nov 1, 2026) — subsidized marketplace enrollees' average annual premium roughly doubled, from $888 to $1,904. CBO projects ~10M combined coverage losses by 2034. A 25-state-and-DC coalition (Massachusetts leads; CA is a co-plaintiff) is suing CMS (Commonwealth of Massachusetts et al. v. Oz, filed June 29, 2026) over the rule's narrowed 'medically frail' exemption — a federal judge denied the coalition's preliminary injunction on July 29, 2026, then on October 29, 2026 vacated the rule's added functional-impairment test for the 'medically frail' exemption (people in the statute's five frailty categories now qualify without it) while upholding its self-attestation and 12-month data-lookback limits. The January 1, 2027 start date stands; on November 13, 2026 CMS let states elect a hold-harmless period through June 30, 2027, during which they must assess compliance but may not deny or disenroll anyone solely for noncompliance (SMD #26-006). A separate Oregon-led four-state suit (filed Nov 5, 2026) challenges the threatened loss of Medicaid funding as unconstitutionally coercive. Full state-by-state breakdown and case studies: Special Topics: Access & Cost under OBBBA →
implications: Georgia Pathways to Coverage (GA Dept of Community Health) is the cautionary preview: GAO found $54.2M spent on admin vs. $26.2M on care, FY2021-Q2 FY2025, with enrollment still far below the ~240,000-250,000-eligible target

Rural hospitals and FQHCs face compounding pressure from coverage loss plus provider-tax/state-directed-payment caps — the $50B Rural Health Transformation Fund is widely expected not to fully offset losses

Medi-Cal plans (San Francisco Health Plan, Partnership HealthPlan of CA) and similar Medicaid MCOs nationally face semi-annual redetermination cycles and rising administrative costs as California's DHCS projects ~1.1M Medi-Cal members losing coverage in its central estimate (up to 3.4M in a higher-end scenario)

CBO, KFF, and Georgetown University's Center for Children and Families (CCF) become the reference infrastructure most states and hospital associations cite for coverage-loss and state-readiness tracking

State AG litigation (Massachusetts-led coalition, CA a co-plaintiff, vs. CMS) has narrowed the medically-frail rule but not halted work requirements — expansion states still implement under protest, so exposure is narrowed and delayed rather than avoided
Covered California and other ACA marketplace administrators face enrollment and affordability pressure independent of OBBBA, from the expired enhanced premium tax credits alone

title: IRA Drug Price Negotiation — Cycle 3 Prices Due Nov 30
catalyst: Cycle 1 prices (10 drugs, 38–79% discounts) took effect Jan 2026, and Cycle 2 prices for 15 more Part D drugs (including semaglutide — Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy) take effect Jan 1, 2027. Cycle 3 — 15 drugs including the first Part B drugs, plus the program's first renegotiation — closed its negotiation period Nov 1, 2026; CMS must publish the resulting maximum fair prices by Nov 30, 2026, effective Jan 1, 2028.
implications: AbbVie, Merck, Amgen face multi-billion annual Medicare revenue reductions
MA/Part D formulary redesign cascades to PBMs (Capital Rx) and MA plans (SCAN, Oscar, Alignment)
Patient access programs (ConnectiveRx, EVERSANA) restructure as out-of-pocket caps shift manufacturer concession math
Regulatory science firms (Certara) see rising demand as pharma builds evidence for price justification
Companion diagnostics (Guardant) tied to negotiated drugs face formulary and access ripple effects

title: CMS-0057-F Prior Auth APIs — Jan 2027 Deadline
catalyst: Two distinct compliance obligations on different timelines: prior authorization decision timeframes compressed to 72 hours (expedited) and 7 days (standard), effective January 1, 2026; separately, four mandated FHIR APIs (prior auth, provider access, payer-to-payer, patient access) covering MA, Medicaid MCOs, and ACA marketplace plans face a January 1, 2027 buildout deadline.
implications: SCAN, Alignment, Oscar, Partnership HealthPlan, SFHP all face mandated API buildout — IT spend rising
Epic's implementation roadmap becomes a critical dependency for health system compliance
Redox and Smile Digital Health positioned as essential middleware; Notable benefits from PA workflow automation volume
Prior auth denial rates likely to fall as transparency increases — downstream revenue risk for utilization management businesses
CHAI AI governance frameworks become more urgent as payers deploy AI for automated prior auth decisions

title: MA Risk Adjustment Tightening (HCC V28 + RADV)
catalyst: HCC V28 model transition reduces average MA risk scores — compressing plan revenue. RADV extrapolation authority was vacated by the Northern District of Texas (Humana v. Becerra, Sept. 25, 2025) on APA grounds; CMS appealed to the Fifth Circuit (No. 25-11293), with briefing ongoing into 2026 and no ruling yet issued — extrapolation is currently enjoined, not in effect. DOJ scrutiny of retrospective chart chase and upcoding continues separately.
implications: SCAN, Alignment, Oscar face revenue headwinds — per-member-per-month margins under pressure
Coding accuracy programs intensify; risk adjustment vendors (Acumen, RTI) see demand rise
Alignment's owned-provider model provides some insulation; pure plan models (Oscar) more exposed
MA enrollment growth may slow as plans exit unprofitable markets or raise premiums
RTI and CMS contractors evaluating whether V28 achieves intended overbilling correction without overcorrection, while the Fifth Circuit appeal leaves extrapolation authority unresolved

title: TEAM Model — Mandatory Episode Accountability
catalyst: CMS mandatory bundled payment model for 5 surgical episode types (joint replacement, hip femur fracture, spinal fusion, CABG, major bowel procedure) at 721 hospitals (revised down from the original 741-hospital list) across 188 core-based statistical areas (CBSAs — which include micropolitan as well as metropolitan areas), running 2026-2030 with no opt-out. Episodes use a 30-day post-discharge window, shorter than CJR/BPCI Advanced's 90-day window. The FY2027 IPPS final rule (released July 31, 2026) finalized CJR-X: mandatory, nationwide 90-day lower-extremity joint replacement episodes from January 1, 2028 for acute care hospitals other than TEAM participants and Maryland hospitals — so the two windows will run side by side in different hospitals.
implications: AdventHealth and other large health systems in selected markets face direct episode risk
Post-acute referral network optimization becomes a financial imperative — SNF and HH quality differentiation is now contractual
August Health (SNF care management) sees premium on PAC coordination capability
Hinge Health surgical decision support adjacent to TEAM joint replacement episodes
Care navigation for ACO REACH beneficiaries overlapping TEAM episodes creates attribution complexity

The Ambulatory Specialty Model (mandatory from Jan 1, 2027) extends CMMI downside risk to individual cardiologists and low-back-pain specialists in roughly one-quarter of CBSAs — the mandatory footprint is widening from hospitals to physicians

title: AI Governance Fragmentation — Federal Floor Contracts as Voluntary Regimes Expand
catalyst: FDA finalized PCCP guidance (Dec 2024) for continuously-learning AI devices. ONC/ASTP finalized HTI-5 on October 26, 2026, removing the AI "model card" source-attribute and risk-management requirements HTI-1 had added to the certified-EHR decision support interventions criterion (the criterion itself was revised, not removed) — a contraction, not an expansion, of the federal mandatory leg. On the voluntary side, the Joint Commission launched its Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare certification on June 1, 2026, building on its Sept 17, 2025 joint guidance with CHAI; it certifies organizations' AI governance, not individual AI products. The mandatory federal floor has contracted while voluntary (CHAI/TJC) and state-level regimes proliferate without reconciliation.
implications: Health systems (Kaiser, Providence, Cleveland Clinic) face a shifting patchwork rather than a stable set of obligations — HTI-5 removed ONC's mandatory model-card transparency requirement for certified EHRs
ModelOp and other CHAI-certified assurance providers compete to operationalize recurring model validation as the de facto trust layer, increasingly by default rather than backstopping a federal floor
Liability for algorithm-driven coverage denials (MA prior-auth) remains unresolved regardless of which regime prevails
State-level AI laws (Utah, Colorado, Texas) add a fourth layer of fragmentation, and become relatively more important now that HTI-5 has narrowed the federal mandatory layer
Notable and other AI-enabled clinical automation vendors must track FDA device rules, ONC's narrowed decision-support certification criterion, and CHAI/Joint Commission certification simultaneously
